etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French parallèle, borrowed from Latin parallelus.

definitions.definition: Equally distant from one another at all points.

quote.text: the instrument held with its plane roughly parallel to the equinoctial or celestial equato

definitions.definition: Having the same overall direction; the comparison is indicated with "to".

quote.citation: 1711 July 2 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison; Richard Steele et al.], “THURSDAY, June 21, 1711”, in The Spectator, number 99; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume II, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: When honour runs parallel with the laws of God and our country, it cannot be too much cherished.The spelling has been modernized.

definitions.definition: (hyperbolic geometry, said of a pair of lines) Either not intersecting, or coinciding.[1]
(computing) Involving the processing of multiple tasks at the same time.
(figuratively) Analogous, similar, comparable.
(science fiction, of realities, dimensions, timelines, etc.) Coexisting but normally not interacting with the regular reality.
With a parallel relationship.
One of a set of parallel lines.

quote.citation: 1733, [Alexander Pope], An Essay on Man. […], (please specify |epistle=I to IV), London: Printed for J[ohn] Wilford, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Who made the spider parallels design, / Sure as De Moivre, without rule or line?

definitions.definition: Direction conformable to that of another line.

quote.text: lines that from their parallel decline

definitions.definition: (geography) A line of latitude.
An arrangement of electrical components such that a current flows along two or more paths; see in parallel.
Something identical or similar in essential respects.

quote.citation: 1728, [Alexander Pope], “Book the Third”, in The Dunciad. An Heroic Poem. […], Dublin, London:  […]  A. Dodd, →OCLC:
quote.text: None but thyself can be thy parallel.

definitions.definition: A comparison made; elaborate tracing of similarity.

(military) One of a series of long trenches constructed before a besieged fortress, by the besieging force, as a cover for troops supporting the attacking batteries. They are roughly parallel to the line of outer defenses of the fortress.
(printing) A character consisting of two parallel vertical lines, used in the text to direct attention to a similarly marked note in the margin or at the foot of a page.
To construct or place something parallel to something else.

quote.citation: 1650, Thomas Browne, Pseudodoxia Epidemica: […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  A[braham] Miller, for Edw[ard] Dod and Nath[aniel] Ekins, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The needle  […]  doth parallel and place itself upon the true meridian.

definitions.definition: Of a path etc: To be parallel to something else.

quote.citation: 1931, H. P. Lovecraft, chapter 6, in The Whisperer in Darkness:
quote.text: Archaic covered bridges lingered fearsomely out of the past in pockets of the hills, and the half-abandoned railway track paralleling the river seemed to exhale a nebulously visible air of desolation.

quote.citation: 2020 December 2, Paul Bigland, “My weirdest and wackiest Rover yet”, in Rail, page 66:
quote.text: Racing on, we parallel the M5 doing 95mph, according to the app on my smartphone.

definitions.definition: Of a process etc: To be analogous to something else.
To compare or liken something to something else.

quote.citation: 1984 April 14, Reginald Shepherd, “White Men's Black Men”, in Gay Community News, page 11:
quote.text: Although its spokesmen do not hesitate to parallel their oppression to that of blacks, the gay male community has chosen to ignore the voices of black gay men.

These scholars argue that gender and sexual identity are like nature and the environment; they parallel the queer/performance connection to the environmental/performance connection. I consider, instead, how all these categories actively interact and overlap.

definitions.definition: To make to conform to something else in character, motive, aim, etc.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Measure for Measure”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: His life is parallelled / Even with the stroke and line of his great justice.

definitions.definition: To equal; to match; to correspond to.

quote.citation: c. 1604–1605 (date written), William Shakespeare, “All’s Well, that Ends Well”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: He will steale sir an Egge out of a Cloister: forrapes and rauishments he paralels Nessus.

definitions.definition: To produce or adduce as a parallel.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii]:
quote.text: My young remembrance cannot parallel / A fellow to it.

quote.citation: 1621, Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy, III.2.2.iv:
quote.text: Who cannot parallel these stories out of his experience?

quote.citation: 1689 December (indicated as 1690), [John Locke], Two Treatises of Government: […], London:  […]  Awnsham Churchill, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Many have exercised their wits in paralleling the inconveniences of regal and popular government
